## Cannabis Law Reform in Aotearoa New Zealand: A History

The story of cannabis regulation in New Zealand stretches back well over a century — from a time when it was freely available at the chemist, to prohibition, a failed legalisation referendum, and ongoing calls for reform.

### Before Prohibition: Widely Available and Cheap

Before the 1920s, cannabis was largely unregulated in New Zealand. It was widely available and inexpensive — reportedly costing about a shilling an ounce (roughly $6 for 30 grams in today's money) — and was an ingredient in many patent medicines and pharmacy preparations. [[1]](cite://1/1) Cannabis was even made exempt from customs duty after 1895. [[2]](cite://2/1)

### Early Restriction: International Pressure Shapes Local Law

It was international conventions, rather than any domestic drug crisis, that first brought cannabis under legal control in New Zealand. A 1924 international convention required restrictions on a growing range of drugs, and New Zealand extended those controls to cannabis (then referred to as "Indian hemp") the following year. [[2]](cite://2/2)

The **Dangerous Drugs Act 1927** then formally placed cannabis on a list of dangerous substances. The minister introducing the legislation actually conceded there was no evidence of extensive drug use in New Zealand — the act was designed to bring the country into line with international standards rather than address a local problem. Under the act, cannabis could only be imported or manufactured under licence, and purchased from a doctor or chemist with a prescription. [[3]](cite://3/1)

In 1955, responding to a World Health Organization request, New Zealand agreed to end cannabis imports altogether. [[4]](cite://4/1)

### The 1960s and the Birth of Recreational Use

Until the mid-1960s there was very little recreational use of, or even knowledge about, cannabis in New Zealand. The arrival of 'hippie' culture changed that dramatically, and police responded by establishing vice squads to combat what was seen as an emerging problem. [[5]](cite://5/1) [[6]](cite://6/1)

### The Misuse of Drugs Act 1975

A key legislative milestone came with the **Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA) 1975**, which prohibited the manufacture, import, supply, or possession of controlled drugs and established a three-tier classification system:

- **Class A** — very high risk of harm
- **Class B** — high risk
- **Class C** — moderate risk

Penalties were assigned according to class, and in 1979 deterrent penalties for drug dealing were increased. [[7]](cite://7/1) An Expert Advisory Committee on Drugs was established in 2000 to evaluate substances and recommend classifications. [[7]](cite://7/2)

By 2010, around 9,000 people were being arrested annually in cannabis seizures alone. [[7]](cite://7/3)

### Growing Calls for Reform in the 1990s and 2000s

The 1990s saw increasing public agitation for a more liberal approach to cannabis. The legalisation advocacy group NORML became active, and in 1996 the Aotearoa Legalise Cannabis Party received 1.6% of the vote in the general election. [[8]](cite://8/1) Surveys through the decade consistently ranked cannabis below alcohol, tobacco, hard drugs, and solvent abuse as a community concern, and a 2000 poll found 56% of respondents wanted the law liberalised. [[8]](cite://8/2)

By the early 2000s, New Zealand had one of the highest rates of cannabis use in the world — roughly half of those aged 15–45 had tried it, about one-fifth had used it in the previous year, and around 15% were current users. [[9]](cite://9/1) [[5]](cite://5/2) Cannabis use was notably higher among Māori than the general population. [[10]](cite://10/1)

### Medicinal Cannabis: A 2020 Law Change

Medicinal cannabis became legal and more readily available following a law change in 2020. Products — ranging from oils to dried flower — must meet minimum quality standards and can be prescribed for pain, sleep, and other conditions. Patients must consult a registered doctor who determines whether psychoactive or non-psychoactive products are appropriate. [[11]](cite://11/1)

Subsequent regulatory changes to the **Misuse of Drugs (Medicinal Cannabis) Regulations** have made it easier for New Zealand growers and manufacturers to export, allowing products to meet the standards of importing nations rather than New Zealand's own quality standards. [[12]](cite://12/1)

### The 2020 Recreational Cannabis Referendum

The most significant recent chapter was the 2020 referendum on a proposed **Cannabis Legalisation and Control Bill**. New Zealanders voted against legalisation — a result that some observers attributed to a persistent cultural wariness around hedonism and drug liberalisation. [[13]](cite://13/1) In October 2025, Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick noted that five years on from the referendum, courts and police resources were still being spent on cannabis prohibition, with 26 people imprisoned for cannabis offences in the previous year alone. [[14]](cite://14/1)

### The Debate Continues

As of late 2025 and into 2026, calls for reform remain active on multiple fronts. The New Zealand Drug Foundation has recommended a complete overhaul of the MDA — calling it a "colossal failure" since its introduction 50 years ago — proposing to scrap the drug classification system and legalise some lower-risk drugs through a not-for-profit model. [[15]](cite://15/1) [[14]](cite://14/2)

The Green Party launched a public consultation platform in October 2025 seeking feedback on what good cannabis regulation might look like, while continuing to advocate for legalisation. [[14]](cite://14/3)

More recently, in April 2026, a member's bill by Green MP Kahurangi Carter — focused on protecting people who call emergency services during a drug overdose from low-level prosecution — passed its first reading in Parliament, reflecting a gradual shift toward viewing drug use as a health issue rather than a criminal one. [[16]](cite://16/1)

The MDA, now over 50 years old, is increasingly viewed by health professionals, researchers, and advocates as outdated — and the debate over what comes next for cannabis law in Aotearoa shows no sign of quieting. [[17]](cite://17/1) [[18]](cite://18/1)

Would you like to explore the specific arguments for and against cannabis legalisation that emerged during the 2020 referendum debate?

7.document_title: Māori Smoking, Alcohol and Drugs: Historical Patterns, Policies, and Health Impacts
7.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines the history, patterns, and health impacts of tobacco, alcohol, and recreational drug use among Māori in New Zealand. Tobacco was introduced by Europeans in the late 1700s and became a standard trade item, with Māori developing significantly higher smoking rates than non-Māori populations—by 1962, 58% of Māori men and 70% of women smoked compared to 38% and 31% in the general population. Alcohol was initially rejected by Māori but gradually adopted from the 1850s onward, prompting government regulations from 1847-1904 restricting Māori access to liquor. Post-WWII restrictions were lifted, leading to increased drinking as urbanization progressed. By the late 20th century, approximately 25% of Māori abstained from alcohol, but those who drank consumed significantly more per session (twice as much in the 1980s), resulting in elevated rates of alcohol-related harm and mortality. Recreational drug use emerged among Māori after WWII, with marijuana becoming common in the 1970s. A 2007-8 survey found 64.6% of Māori aged 16-64 had used drugs recreationally—higher than any other ethnic group—with concerning patterns of early initiation and elevated usage rates for cannabis, BZP party pills, amphetamines, and methamphetamine. The document details community-level interventions, including dry zones, and quit-smoking programmes implemented to address these interconnected public health issues.

10.document_title: New Zealand Liquor Laws: Comprehensive History and Legislative Reforms from 1840 to 2012
10.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand's liquor laws spanning over 170 years, from 1840 through 2012. It covers early licensing systems adopted from Britain, the Licensing Act 1881 which standardized laws nationally, and the temperance movement's influence leading to prohibition referendums between 1911-1987. Key historical developments include discriminatory laws against Māori (repealed 1948), restrictions on women holding licenses (until 1952), and raising the drinking age to 21 (1910). The document details six o'clock closing in bars (1917), licensing trusts in former dry areas (1943), and prohibition referendums with near-success rates. The 1960s-70s liberalization period saw restaurants allowed to sell alcohol and extended bar hours. 18.document_title: Garden Remedy: Mother Aubert's Homemade Medicine
18.document_summary: This article explores the historical use of cannabis in 19th-century New Zealand medicine. Before the Dangerous Drugs Act of 1927, cannabis was a legal and affordable ingredient in patent medicines, including "Indian hemp" remedies for asthma, coughs, and menstrual cramps. Mother Suzanne Aubert, a French-born nun and trained nurse, was one of New Zealand's earliest cannabis cultivators. At her home for the disadvantaged at Hiruharama on the Whanganui River, she grew cannabis and created commercial remedies like 'Paramo', 'Marupa', and 'Wanena'. After licensing her recipes to the New Zealand Drug Company in 1891, quality declined, and Aubert reportedly destroyed remaining stock and recipes. She later moved to Wellington, establishing multiple charitable institutions including a medical training school and soup kitchen still operating today.

Fischer argues that the U.S. was founded on principles of individual liberty and freedom from government control, stemming from oppressive British colonial rule (1630-1783), while New Zealand developed under more benevolent British administration in the 1830s, leading to a national emphasis on fairness and social justice. [Page 1] “We are everywhere” By Vaughan Yarwood The fight to decriminalise homosexuality. If there were such a thing as a social seismograph—a piece of tech that recorded the collisions and ruptures caused by deep seated movement in New Zealand society—it would have been off the charts in the 1980s. Shock after shock brought a usually restrained public out onto streets, playing fields and harbours. There was the Springbok rugby tour of 1981, French nuclear tests in the Pacific, and, in 1985, the Homosexual Law Reform Bill. Homosexuality had long been considered immoral and unnatural in Britain and its colonies, and buggery was punishable by death. In 1893, following changes in English law, New Zealand extended prohibitions to include any sexual activity between men and replaced the death penalty with flogging and imprisonment for life with hard labour. Consent was no defence. (Sex between women has never been illegal in this country.) It wasn’t until almost 70 years later that attempts were made to repeal the legislation, or at least reduce its severity. In 1959, Attorney General Rex Mason tried unsuccessfully to soften the sanctions on some homosexual activities—spurred, some say, by the suicide of a gay acquaintance. The Crimes Act 1961 did away with the threat of life imprisonment for sodomy, but still kept it illegal. Impatient for change, in 1967 activists in Wellington formed the New Zealand Homosexual Law Reform Society and invited former governor general Lord Cobham to be its patron. His forthright reply signalled the difficulties ahead. “These people are sick,” he said. “The whole problem of legalising this offence seems to me to hinge upon the extent to which the disease is contagious.” It was to be a common refrain: if not contained, homosexuality would destroy the family, spread AIDS, and erode the very fabric of society. Some even conflated homosexuality with paedophilia. Well meaning proposed legislation in the 1970s didn’t go far enough for gay liberation groups, which demanded total equality, including in the contentious area of age of consent. Then in March 1985, Fran Wilde, MP for Wellington Central, introduced the Homosexual Law Reform Bill. This private member’s bill, in two parts, aimed to decriminalise consensual male homosexual practices, and to end discrimination for both men and women on the grounds of sexual orientation. Opposition was fierce—a petition against the bill delivered to Parliament in September contained some 800,000 signatures. Finally, on the evening of July 9, 1986, came the bill’s third reading. It was a Wednesday. Outside Parliament, a group of Catholics prayed before a glass cased statue of Mary, as they had so often over the previous 18 months, their faces lit by kerosene lanterns. In the House, tension was palpable. “Every seat was taken, most by lesbians, gay men and our friends,” recalled one of the movement’s chroniclers, Hugh Young. “Stern looking opponents—many of the women in the headscarves of the Exclusive Brethren—sat in the Speaker’s Gallery.” Then came the sound of the division bell. Time to vote. The previous week, the campaign had almost ended in disaster when a number of sympathetic MPs were stranded by bad weather. Only MP George Gair’s deciding vote against a closure motion that would have led to an immediate vote on the bill kept it alive. This time, the Speaker, Gerry Wall, announced that the bill was passed into law by a margin of five votes, prompting wild cheers and hugs from the galleries. After a short speech, Wilde headed to her office with supporters to celebrate with, it is said, at least one bottle of Château Le Gay.

The narrative details failed control attempts including ferrets, stoats, and weasels, followed by the "Killer Policy" of 1938 using strychnine and 1080 poison. By the 1990s, government subsidy cuts left 72% of affected properties running cash deficits. The document examines the 1997 biosecurity breach when farmers illegally smuggled RCD into the country, with figures like Donald Young, Bruce Jolly, and Pete Davis secretly breeding infected rabbits. It discusses the virus's origins in China, its spread through Australia, and the complex scientific and ethical debates between government agencies, conservation groups, and farming communities. While the virus initially achieved dramatic population reductions and was legalized in 1999, immunity levels in rabbit populations have reached 90% in some areas, resulting in mixed long-term effectiveness.

46.document_summary: The Harm Reduction Coalition and drug policy advocates are calling for radical reform of New Zealand's Misuse of Drugs Act, marking 50 years since its enactment. Researchers, including Dr. Fiona Hutton and Dr. Julian Buchanan, argue that decades of drug prohibition have failed to reduce drug use or criminal trade. They advocate for repealing the current act and establishing new legislation that treats drugs as a health issue under the Ministry of Health rather than the justice system, with differentiated regulations based on drug-specific harms. Evidence from Portugal's decriminalization success is cited. However, the government has rejected liberalizing drug laws, instead announcing a $30 million methamphetamine crackdown with increased police enforcement and a media campaign. Mental Health Minister Matt Doocey emphasizes a health-led response balancing enforcement, prevention, and treatment, with $246 million invested in addiction services.

1.fileDescription: This article explores the historical use of cannabis in 19th-century New Zealand medicine. Before the Dangerous Drugs Act of 1927, cannabis was a legal and affordable ingredient in patent medicines, including "Indian hemp" remedies for asthma, coughs, and menstrual cramps. Mother Suzanne Aubert, a French-born nun and trained nurse, was one of New Zealand's earliest cannabis cultivators. At her home for the disadvantaged at Hiruharama on the Whanganui River, she grew cannabis and created commercial remedies like 'Paramo', 'Marupa', and 'Wanena'. 10.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines the history, patterns, and health impacts of tobacco, alcohol, and recreational drug use among Māori in New Zealand. Tobacco was introduced by Europeans in the late 1700s and became a standard trade item, with Māori developing significantly higher smoking rates than non-Māori populations—by 1962, 58% of Māori men and 70% of women smoked compared to 38% and 31% in the general population. Alcohol was initially rejected by Māori but gradually adopted from the 1850s onward, prompting government regulations from 1847-1904 restricting Māori access to liquor. Post-WWII restrictions were lifted, leading to increased drinking as urbanization progressed. By the late 20th century, approximately 25% of Māori abstained from alcohol, but those who drank consumed significantly more per session (twice as much in the 1980s), resulting in elevated rates of alcohol-related harm and mortality. Recreational drug use emerged among Māori after WWII, with marijuana becoming common in the 1970s. A 2007-8 survey found 64.6% of Māori aged 16-64 had used drugs recreationally—higher than any other ethnic group—with concerning patterns of early initiation and elevated usage rates for cannabis, BZP party pills, amphetamines, and methamphetamine. The document details community-level interventions, including dry zones, and quit-smoking programmes implemented to address these interconnected public health issues.

chunkHighlights.text: Drugs in recreational use in New Zealand in the 2000s included cannabis, ecstasy, amphetamines, prescription stimulants, synthetic and naturally occurring hallucinogens, ketamine, GHB, nitrous oxide and BZP (benzylpiperazine) party pills. Marijuana and BZP party pills were the drugs of choice among Māori, who used both at a higher rate than the population as a whole. In 2012 the United Nations reported that use of marijuana was particularly high in Oceania (which includes New Zealand, Australia and the Pacific Islands) – 9–15% of the population, compared to 3–5% worldwide – so the rate of use by Māori was amongst the highest in the world.

Party pills containing BZP were introduced to New Zealand in 2000. They were made a restricted substance in 2005 and became illegal in 2008. Prior to this, 23% of Māori adults had tried them, compared with 14.4% of Europeans (the group with the next-highest rate of use).

13.fileDescription: This article examines New Zealand's 50-year experiment with alcohol prohibition and restricted drinking hours. Beginning in 1917 during World War I, the government implemented a 6pm closing time for bars as a compromise to full prohibition, intended to keep workers sober and productive. The policy, meant to be temporary, became permanent in 1918 and remained until 1967. During this period, men would rush to pubs at 5pm to consume as much alcohol as possible within the one-hour window, leading to widespread intoxication and social problems through the Great Depression and World War II. The article notes that returning servicemen exposed to European moderate drinking culture and international tourists contributed to changing attitudes. The 6pm closing was finally repealed on October 9, 1967, following a nationwide referendum. The piece reflects on New Zealand's historical puritanical attitudes toward hedonism and excess, contrasting them with modern perspectives on drug policy liberalization.

17.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines cannabis policy, enforcement, and use in New Zealand through multiple interconnected perspectives. It profiles individuals like Steve Wilson, a chronic pain sufferer using cannabis to manage central sensitization syndrome, and Kate Kennedy, whose cannabis use led to psychotic episodes, illustrating the tension between medicinal necessity and health risks. The document analyzes New Zealand's evolving cannabis landscape: nearly half of adults have tried cannabis, with 79% supporting its use for pain relief and 82% for terminal illness, yet the country maintains strict prohibition under a 40-year-old Misuse of Drugs Act. Police enforcement efforts are substantial—spending $90 million annually on cannabis enforcement with operations like Operation Dee seizing 132,000 plants and arresting 572 people. Treasury analysis projects potential tax revenue of $150 million annually from legal cannabis sales, while enforcement costs reach $109 million for courts and justice. The document explores the "entourage effect" theory, international public health guidelines recommending moderate consumption, and the disproportionate impact of enforcement on Māori communities. It presents cannabis simultaneously as a medical breakthrough for chronic pain management, an engine of gang economy, and a potential tax revenue source, while questioning New Zealand's prohibition approach compared to international law changes.
